item.title: A 25% off Etsy sale can cut your profit nearly in half. Here's the Black Friday maths
item.description: On a $40 item that costs you $16 to make, Etsy's fees leave you $19.75 at full price. At 25% off, you keep $10.70. That means you need about 85% more orders just to make the same money. Here's the sum, and how to choose a discount that still pays.
item.content:encoded:
The short version: On a $40 Etsy item, a 25% off sale can drop what you keep from $19.75 to $10.70. Your costs stay the same while the price falls, so profit falls by almost half, and you'd need about 85% more orders to stand still. Before you set a Black Friday discount, work out what each sale will leave you. It takes about two minutes.

The sum at full price

Take a $40 item with free shipping. Say it costs you $16 all in: materials, packaging, postage and your time. If your $16 leaves out postage or labour, the amount left below is before those costs, not profit.

Our example assumes a US seller paid in dollars, one item per order, no gift wrap and no sales tax. Etsy's fee pages set three charges for that seller:

  • Transaction fee: 6.5% of the price the buyer pays after your discount, so $2.60.
  • Payment processing: 3% plus $0.25, so $1.45.
  • Listing fee: $0.20, charged again when a listing with more stock sells and renews.

That's $4.25 in fees. You keep $19.75.

The same item at 25% off

At 25% off, the price is $30. The fees shrink a little, to $3.30, because two of them are percentages. But your $16 making cost doesn't shrink at all.

You keep $10.70. The price fell by a quarter. Your profit fell by 46%.

The part most sellers miss

To make the same money at 25% off, you need about 85% more orders. If you usually sell 20 of this item in Black Friday week, you'd need about 37 at the sale price to match.

Ads make it tighter. If a buyer clicks one of Etsy's Offsite Ads and orders within 30 days, Etsy charges 15% of the order, capped at $100. Shops that pass $10,000 in sales over 365 days pay 12% instead.

Below that level you can opt out of Offsite Ads in your shop settings. Above it, the ads are compulsory.

On the $30 sale, the 15% rate takes another $4.50, and you'd keep $6.20.

These figures leave out sales tax. The processing fee is charged on the whole order, including tax and any shipping you charge, and the transaction fee covers charged shipping too. With free shipping, as here, only tax adds to the fees.

The 25% question

Etsy's own Cyber Specials event runs November 23 to December 1. To be considered for Etsy's marketing, a shop had to opt in by October 27 with at least 25% off. That deadline has passed.

So 25% is the number many sellers copy, but it only bought a chance at Etsy's promotion. A shop that missed the opt-in can still run its own sale at any discount it chooses. On low-margin items, a smaller discount may keep more money than a bigger one.

What to do this week

  1. Run your own numbers for your three best sellers in our free Etsy fee calculator. Include postage and your time in the cost.
  2. Compare four prices for each: no discount, 10%, 15% and 25%. Note what each sale leaves you.
  3. Work out the orders you'd need: divide your full-price profit by your sale-price profit, then multiply by your usual orders.
  4. Count your Offsite Ads sales from last year's holiday season, so you know how many may carry the extra fee.

What's still unknown: how many extra orders a sale brings in. That depends on your shop, and last year's Black Friday numbers are your best guide.

What we checked: Etsy's Fees & Payments Policy and its Etsy Payments Policy, read on November 5, 2026, with the fees page rechecked on November 9. We also read Etsy's Holiday HQ page for the Cyber Specials rules. All are listed below. The $40 item and $16 cost are our own worked example.

item.title: Printful and Printify's $0.40 holiday surcharge: who pays it, and how to cover it
item.description: Both print-on-demand suppliers charge sellers a $0.40 holiday shipping surcharge on each order to a US address, from October 15, 2026, to January 17, 2027. It isn't added to your storefront prices automatically, so unless your prices already cover it, it comes out of your margin. Here's what it costs, and how to pass it on.
item.content:encoded:
The short version: If you sell through Printful or Printify, each order you ship to a US address costs you an extra $0.40 until January 17, 2027. Both suppliers charge it to you, the seller, and neither adds it to your storefront prices automatically. Unless you've raised your prices, it's coming out of your margin on every US order right now. The one exception: Printify orders that use TikTok Shipping.

Forty cents sounds small. Across a busy holiday season, it isn't.

Which orders it applies to

Both suppliers charge the surcharge from October 15, 2026, to January 17, 2027, on orders shipped to US addresses, whatever the shipping method. It's charged once per order. Printful says that holds even when an order ships in more than one parcel, and Printify says the same when several print providers fulfil one order.

Both say they add it every holiday season, in line with the peak-season surcharges US carriers charge.

What it costs a small shop

The surcharge is flat, so it adds up with your order count, not your order size.

  • 100 orders in the season: $40.
  • 500 orders: $200.
  • 1,000 orders: $400.

It hurts most on low-profit orders. On an order that makes you $2, 40 cents is a fifth of your profit.

How to pass it on

Printful. If you use Shopify flat rates or Printful's live shipping rates (on Shopify, WooCommerce, Ecwid or a custom store), go to Dashboard, then Settings, then Store settings, then Shipping. Under "Temporary shipping surcharges", tick "Add surcharges to shipping prices on my storefront."

Etsy with Printful. Create a new shipping profile, or duplicate a Printful-generated one, add $0.40 to your US rates, and move your listings onto it. Printful says its own generated profiles get overwritten when products update, so changes made there won't last.

Printify. Raise your product prices in Printify, then republish the products so the change reaches your store.

Two more details. Printful says sales tax applies to the surcharge in states where shipping is taxable, and coupons and shipping discounts don't cover it. Printify refunds the surcharge if an order is fully cancelled, but keeps it on a partial cancellation.

What to do this week

  1. Check a recent US order for the surcharge in its shipping cost.
  2. Decide which products need it passed on, starting with your lowest-profit ones. Remember marketplace fees take a cut of anything you add.
  3. Make the change using the steps above for your platform.
  4. Re-run your prices with our free print-on-demand profit calculator.
  5. Set a reminder for January 18 to take the $0.40 back out of your prices.

What's still unknown: the help pages don't say what next season's surcharge will be. We'll update this story if either supplier changes it before January 17.

What we checked: Printful's and Printify's help pages on the 2026 holiday shipping surcharge, read on November 4, 2026. Both are listed below.

item.title: TikTok Shop's Black Friday sale runs November 11–30. Here's who can join, and the catch on returns
item.description: TikTok Shop's Black Friday and Cyber Monday campaign runs from November 11 to 30. Most shops need a performance score of at least 3.5 to get in. And eligible purchases sold from November 11 to December 31 can be returned until February 10, 2027. Here's what that means for your cash and your stock.
item.content:encoded:
The short version: Holiday sales on TikTok Shop can come back to you until February 10, 2027. That's the return deadline for eligible purchases in TikTok Shop's Black Friday and Cyber Monday campaign, which runs from November 11 to 30, Pacific time. To get your products in, your shop has to meet TikTok's health scores, and most campaign applications take 5 to 14 business days to review. A shop that applies today may only get in partway through the sale, so apply now.

Who can get in

TikTok's seller guide sets the bar. Your Shop Performance Score needs to be 3.5 or higher. Your late dispatch rate over the last 30 days must be 20% or lower, and your account health rating "should ideally be above 150."

New shops without a score are checked for fewer than three serious violations in the last 30 days. Products need a low complaint rate, accurate listings, and stock that is ready to ship.

You register in Seller Center, under Marketing, then Campaigns. TikTok says most campaign applications are reviewed in 5 to 14 business days, and it keeps checking eligibility during the campaign, so a shop whose scores drop can lose its place.

The catch on returns

Holiday returns run long this year. TikTok's guide says eligible purchases sold from November 11 (4pm Pacific) to December 31 can be returned until February 10, 2027. Auction orders are left out, and some categories, such as electronics and jewelry, may keep their standard rules.

So don't spend all your holiday sales money in December. Keep some aside for returns, and keep track of which products come back most.

There's a second catch on price. TikTok says many of your own promotions, such as extra discounts or flash deals, don't stack on top of campaign pricing. Strike-through prices only show when the campaign price is below your regular price.

Shipping gets a little slack

TikTok is giving sellers extra time to ship. For local shipping, dispatch and delivery deadlines move by one business day for orders from November 11 to 24, by two business days for orders from November 25 to December 1, and by one business day for orders from December 2 to 5.

The extension doesn't cover pre-orders or back orders.

For affiliate creators

TikTok's guide says some creator campaigns need the product registered in a product campaign first. If you promote a shop's products, ask the shop now whether it has applied, and confirm the commission you've agreed. Creators have their own health scores too, so check yours in the creator center before the sale starts.

What to do this week

  1. Check your Shop Performance Score and late dispatch rate in Seller Center before you apply.
  2. Apply under Marketing, then Campaigns, now, since review can take up to 14 business days.
  3. Set your campaign price below your regular price, and don't count on extra discounts stacking on top.
  4. Work out your margin on each product after the discount, shipping and expected returns, and set some of your holiday sales aside for returns until February 10.
  5. Creators: ask your shops which products are registered. Our free affiliate earnings calculator shows what a sale pays you.

What's still unknown: TikTok's guide doesn't give a minimum discount or a firm registration deadline. Check Seller Center for the exact terms on your shop.

item.title: The EU's new €2 parcel fee is live. A three-item order can now carry €15 in charges
item.description: Since November 1, online orders shipped into the EU from outside it carry a €2 handling fee for each distinct item, on top of July's €3 duty. It's counted by item, not by parcel, and it isn't refunded on returns. Here's what it adds to an order, using the tax office's own examples, and who ends up paying.
item.content:encoded:
The short version: If you ship orders to EU buyers from the US or anywhere else outside the EU, your margin on those orders just shrank. Since November 1, each order carries a €2 handling fee for every distinct item in it, on top of the €3 customs duty the EU added in July. It's counted by item, not by parcel, and it isn't refunded if the buyer sends the order back.

On a single mug, that's €5 of charges before VAT. On Irish Revenue's example of a pen, a notebook and a key ring in one parcel, it's €15.

How the EU counts it

The Irish tax office, Revenue, has published worked examples. Two identical pens count as one item: €3 of duty and €2 of handling, so €5 plus any VAT.

A pen, a notebook and a key ring in one €10 parcel count as three items. That's €9 of duty and €6 of handling, so €15 plus any VAT.

That's why a cheap add-on can cost more than it sells for. Customs counts an "item" by its tariff classification, so different kinds of product usually count separately, while several of the same product count once.

The handling fee also applies to bigger orders. Above €150, the flat €3 duty gives way to normal duty rates, but the €2 per item still applies. Revenue's example: jeans and runners worth €250 pay €37.35 in duty and €4 in handling. Gifts sent from one private person to another are left out.

The part most sellers miss

Revenue says the fee is aimed at "the platform, marketplaces and businesses involved in bringing eCommerce packages into the EU, rather than being designed as a direct charge on the consumer." In practice, someone pays it. If your checkout doesn't collect it, the buyer can be asked for it when the parcel arrives, and that's a poor first impression for your shop.

Revenue is plain about refunds: "The UHF is non-refundable, even when goods are faulty or returned." What counts is where the parcel ships from, not where you're based. A US shop that fulfils from a warehouse inside the EU isn't caught by it.

What to do this week

  1. Check how your platform handles EU orders. Look in your marketplace's or shipping app's settings for whether import charges are collected at checkout or left for the buyer to pay on delivery.
  2. Recalculate your EU margin by item, not by parcel. Use the examples above as a guide, then allow for returns, since the fee isn't refunded. Our free price calculator for dropshippers lets you add the charges as a cost.
  3. Ask your print-on-demand or dropshipping supplier where EU orders ship from, and whether one order can leave in more than one parcel.
  4. Say it on your shipping page, so EU buyers aren't surprised at the door.

What's still unknown: Revenue's pages don't say exactly how each carrier and platform collects the fee, and other EU countries may publish their own guidance. We'll update this story when they do.

What we checked: Irish Revenue's two Union Handling Fee pages, read on November 2, 2026, and the European Commission's July notice on the €3 duty. All three are listed below.

item.title: eBay payouts go on-demand by default from November 4. Here's the setting to check
item.description: From Wednesday, November 4, eBay starts gradually moving eligible US sellers onto 'eBay balance', where payouts are on demand by default. Automatic daily, weekly, biweekly and monthly payouts are still there, but you may have to choose one again. Here's how to tell, and what to set.
item.content:encoded:
The short version: If you sell on eBay in the US, your sales money may stop landing in your bank on its own once eBay balance is switched on for your account. eBay starts that rollout gradually on Wednesday, November 4, and payouts under eBay balance are on demand by default. If you rely on a daily or weekly payout, check your schedule as soon as eBay tells you the change has reached your account.

Using your balance adds no fee, and your selling fees stay the same. What changes is when the money moves, and in the busiest selling weeks of the year, that's the money that pays for your postage and your stock.

What eBay is changing

eBay's new balance terms take effect for existing balance users on November 4, and apply to new sellers enrolled on or after October 21 once they accept them. eBay's help page says it is introducing eBay balance gradually to eligible US private sellers and sole proprietors, and that it will notify you when it's on for your account. So not everyone changes on Wednesday.

Once it's on, your sales money goes into your eBay balance first. eBay's terms say funds usually become available within two business days, though timing can vary. From there, on-demand is the default: you press withdraw when you want the money. If you never ask for a withdrawal, the terms say eBay pays out your available funds no more than 330 days after your most recent sale.

That's a long time for holiday money to sit still.

The thing most sellers will miss

Value Added Resource, which reported eBay's October 20 notice to sellers, says shops already on a daily, weekly, biweekly or monthly schedule are reset to on-demand when they're enrolled. eBay's own pages confirm on-demand is the default but don't spell out the reset, so check your schedule after you're enrolled and set it again if it has changed.

There's a second catch. Daily payouts switch off on-demand withdrawals. Weekly, biweekly and monthly schedules let you do both. If you like to pull money out early for a big postage run, a weekly schedule keeps that option open.

What the balance is, and isn't

You can spend your eBay balance on eBay itself, including shipping labels and promoted listings, with no extra fee. It doesn't earn interest, and the terms say it isn't covered by FDIC pass-through insurance. It isn't a bank account. Funds marked "On hold" aren't counted in your balance and can't be spent or withdrawn.

Getting money out quickly costs extra. eBay lists a $2.00 flat fee for each express payout to an eligible bank account or debit card, which usually arrives within 30 minutes. A standard payout usually reaches your bank 1 to 3 business days after you start it. eBay's terms add that withdrawals can take up to 12 hours to switch on at first.

What to do this week

  1. Watch for eBay's notice that eBay balance is on for your account.
  2. Open Seller Hub, go to Payments, then Payout settings, and pick daily, weekly, biweekly or monthly. Weekly payouts start on Tuesdays.
  3. Finish identity verification if eBay asks. Sellers who don't pass can't receive payouts until they do.
  4. Plan your postage money. If you buy labels from your balance, leave enough in it for the next few days of orders. Our free cash-flow forecaster for resellers shows when money comes in and goes out.

What's still unknown: eBay hasn't said when every account will be switched over, and its help pages still show some older wording about daily payouts. We'll update this story if that changes.

What we checked: eBay's balance Terms and Conditions and its help page on getting paid, both read on November 2, 2026, and Value Added Resource's report of eBay's October 20 notice. All three are listed below.

item.title: Etsy's new photo rule: one real, unedited picture for most products. Here's who has to fix what
item.description: Etsy now wants at least one unedited photo of the actual item on most listings, and it bans AI-written patterns and recipes. If a listing already has a qualifying photo, you may not need anything new. Here's how to tell which listings are at risk before a holiday buyer finds out for you.
item.content:encoded:
The short version: On October 22 Etsy changed its rules on listing photos and AI. Most listings now need at least one photo of the actual item, against a real background, that hasn't been edited at all. Patterns, recipes and instructions written by AI are no longer allowed. If a listing doesn't meet the image rules and a buyer opens a case because the item is materially different, you may be the one paying the refund.

If you sell handmade or vintage goods, you probably took real photos already. The question is whether one of them is still untouched, or whether every picture has been through a filter, a background remover or an AI "enhance" button. With holiday orders about to start, this is the week to check.

Who may already be fine: shops whose listings each include an accurate, unedited photo of the actual item on a real background. If a production partner prints your original design on a standard product, a stock mockup you're authorized to use is allowed. Audio and other downloads with nothing to see can use representative images, as long as they don't mislead. Every other rule below still applies.

What Etsy actually changed

There are three rules, and they don't all hit the same shops.

One untouched photo. For most products, a listing must include at least one unedited photo of the actual item against a real background. Etsy means unedited literally: no crop, no color fix, nothing. Your other photos can still be edited, including with AI, as long as the item still looks like what arrives.

No AI-written guides. If you sell a pattern, a recipe or instructions, the part buyers rely on must be your own work. Patterns, recipes, seeds and similar products also need at least one real, unedited photo of a result made with them: the finished sweater, the baked cake, the flower grown from your seeds.

No bot-made listings. Listings created with no human involvement will be removed, and Etsy says the shop can go with them.

AI art itself is still allowed if you played a clear creative role, you disclose it, and you don't present it as handmade or entirely your own.

The real risk is the refund, not the robot

Most coverage has focused on Etsy's new detection tools. Those are real. Etsy is also adding a way for members to report misleading AI images, and to start, those reports help Etsy understand the problem and won't result in immediate enforcement. Etsy can still remove misleading listings, and repeated violations can go as far as shop removal.

The sharper edge is quieter. If your listing doesn't meet the image rules and a buyer opens a case saying the item is "materially different", Etsy may refund the buyer and you may be responsible for the amount. That's a refund on an order you already shipped, often in December, when you have the most orders.

So the useful question isn't "will Etsy catch me?" It's "if a buyer complains, can my listing show the item as it really is?"

Which listings to look at first

Etsy's exceptions decide a lot, so sort your listings before you touch a camera.

What you sellWhat Etsy asks for
Handmade or vintage items you can photographAt least one unedited photo of the real item on a real background
Your original design printed by a production partner on a standard productA stock mockup is allowed if its owner has authorized your use
Custom pieces you make yourselfReal photos of finished pieces you've made before
Patterns, recipes, seeds and similarAt least one real, unedited photo of a result made with it; AI images can't be the only ones
Digital downloadsA preview or excerpt of the real file; downloads with nothing visual can use representative images that don't mislead

Start with your best sellers, then anything whose photos all came out of an editing app. Pattern and recipe shops that used AI to write the content have the biggest job. Adding a real photo won't fix that. The guide itself has to be your own work.

One point that's easy to miss: Etsy doesn't require the unedited photo to be first. Its advice is that your first photo should be the clearest, most realistic view of the item, because that's the one buyers see in search. If your first image is already honest, you can add the plain shot further along.

Choosing that first photo, one that earns the click and still looks exactly like what arrives, is a chapter of Etsy Basics.

What to do this week

  1. Sort your listings using the table above, and note the ones that are missing the photo Etsy asks for.
  2. Add what your row asks for. For most physical items, that's a photo of the real item on a real background, not edited or changed in any way. For patterns, recipes and seeds, it's a real, unedited photo of a result. For print-on-demand and digital downloads, follow the table.
  3. If you sell patterns or recipes, check that the content is your own work and that one listing photo is a real, unedited photo of a finished result.
  4. Keep your other photos honest. Lighting, exposure and color balance are fine if they match real life; crops and background changes are fine if the item stays accurate. Don't change its actual color, texture or condition, or hide damage. If you used AI to edit any photos, Etsy suggests noting in the description that the images were edited.
  5. Before your next batch of listings, work through our free "human half" worksheet, which covers the photo side of a listing: the lead image and the photos that make a stranger trust it.

One date for later: California, January 1

Etsy's announcement also flags a California law, SB 1050, that takes effect on January 1, 2027. If your listing images or videos prominently feature an AI-generated synthetic performer (a realistic human-looking figure or voice that isn't an identifiable real person), they may count as advertisements and may need a clear disclosure. Etsy suggests considering whether you need one and asking your own lawyer.

We'll watch for what Etsy said it will explore next: ways to tell buyers when AI has been used. Earlier from the desk: this year's holiday shipping dates, and how to find your own last order day.

item.title: What changed for online sellers in 2026: the worries, the wins, and who it hits
item.description: Ten months in, the main fee you pay when something sells has stood still. Postage, parcels to Europe, eBay payouts and Etsy's photo rules are where 2026 moved. Here's what each change means for a small shop, in plain English.
item.content:encoded:
The short version: If you sell on Etsy, eBay or Mercari, the main fee you pay when something sells is the same today as it was in January. What moved this year is everything around the sale. USPS changed its prices four times, Europe added new charges on parcels, eBay changes how you get paid next week, and Etsy rewrote its photo rules.

None of it is a reason to panic. Most of it is a reason to spend one quiet evening checking your prices.

Find your shop first

Each row is one kind of shop, what changed for it, and the one thing to do, with the date it matters by.

If you...What changed for youDo this, by when
Sell physical items on EtsyOne unedited photo per listing; postage upAdd the photo to best sellers this week; reprice shipping before December
Sell patterns, recipes or other downloads on EtsyAI-written guides banned; a test lets buyers order printed copiesCheck your guides are your own work now; opt out of the print test if you'd rather
Resell on eBayPayout schedules may switch to on-demand from November 4After November 4, check your payout schedule in Seller Hub
Resell on MercariPrepaid label prices changed three timesRecheck what you charge on heavier items this week
Sell print on demandA 40-cent holiday surcharge on US ordersAdd it to shipping, or price it in, until January 17
Ship to buyers in the EU€3 duty since July; €2 handling fee from November 1Decide who pays before November 1
Sell less than $20,000 a yearYou usually won't get a 1099-K formKeep your records anyway

Who can ignore most of this: US shops that sell only downloads that aren't patterns or recipes. The postage and Europe changes don't touch you. Read your row, then skip to the good news.

The fees held still. The cost of getting a parcel there didn't.

Etsy's transaction fee is still 6.5% and a listing still costs 20 cents. Etsy revised its fee policy on October 5 without changing either one. eBay's and Mercari's main selling fees for US sellers haven't moved either.

So if you've been bracing for a fee hike, it hasn't come. The money went somewhere else: the label.

USPS raised its prices on January 18. On April 26 it added a temporary 8% on its main parcel services, which runs until January 17, 2027.

On July 12 it changed how some business label prices are worked out, including for parcels under a pound and for large, light boxes. Then, from October 4, a holiday increase landed on top, also until January 17.

Here's what that means for one order. Say a label cost you $6.00 last year, and you still charge $6.00 for shipping. The 8% on its own adds about 48 cents, before the January and holiday changes.

Etsy also takes 6.5% of what the buyer pays for shipping, which is 39 cents on $6.00. So that $6.00 charge now leaves you well short of what the label costs, and the gap comes out of your profit on every order.

That's the thing most sellers miss this year. The price list on the marketplace looks the same, so it feels like nothing changed. Your margin changed anyway. Etsy Basics walks through setting a shipping price that covers the label and the fee charged on it.

The worrying side

Four changes cost money, or catch people out if they don't know about them.

Mercari labels and print partners. Mercari's prepaid labels changed on January 20, again on May 7 to add the USPS surcharge, and again for some weights on October 19. Print partners Printful and Printify add 40 cents to each US order from October 15 to January 17.

Parcels to Europe. Since July 1 the EU has charged a €3 customs duty on low-value parcels from outside the EU. From November 1 it adds a €2 handling fee. Both are charged once for each different product in the parcel, not for each copy.

So a parcel with two identical mugs counts as one product: €3 of duty and €2 of handling. A parcel with a pen, a notebook and a key ring counts as three: €9 and €6. The handling fee isn't refunded if the buyer sends the parcel back. If you sell to EU buyers, decide before November 1 whether those charges go into your price or come out of your margin.

eBay payouts. eBay's new balance terms take effect for existing US sellers on November 4. Value Added Resource, which reported eBay's notice to sellers, says payout schedules switch to on-demand once a seller is enrolled. Daily, weekly and monthly payouts are still available. You just have to set yours again after November 4, or your money waits at eBay until you ask for it.

Etsy's photo and AI rules. Since October 22, most Etsy listings need at least one unedited photo of the real item on a real background. Print-on-demand items can use a stock mockup you're allowed to use, and downloads have their own rules. AI-written patterns and recipes are banned. The risk to watch: if a listing misses the rules and a buyer opens a case saying the item is different, Etsy may refund the buyer and you may be the one paying.

The good side

The $600 tax form isn't coming. For years, sellers were told that marketplaces and payment apps would send a Form 1099-K once sales passed $600. A 2025 law moved the line back to more than $20,000 and more than 200 sales in a year. A platform can still send one for less, and some states set lower limits. You owe tax on your profit either way.

Etsy is paying back more of its fee for the holidays. Until January 4, invited sellers in Etsy's Share & Save program get the full 6.5% transaction fee back on eligible sales that come through their own shared links. The usual refund is 4%.

Etsy's buyer protection got bigger. Since May 7, Etsy's Purchase Protection covers up to $250 of the refund on eligible orders of any size. Before, only orders of $250 or less were covered. That's a real help on the day a parcel goes missing.

What to do this week

  1. Reprice shipping against today's postage, not last year's.
  2. Shipping to the EU: decide before November 1 who pays the new charges.
  3. Etsy sellers: add one unedited photo to your best sellers, then work down the list.
  4. eBay sellers: after November 4, open Seller Hub, go to Payments, and set your payout schedule.
  5. In Share & Save? Share your links now, while the refund is the full 6.5%.

To see what one order really leaves you after Etsy's fees and your new postage, run it through our free fee calculator.

What we're still watching

Several seller guides report that TikTok Shop raised its US referral fee from 6% to 8% in August. TikTok's own public fee table still showed 6% when it was last checked, so we haven't counted it here. If you sell there, your settlement statement is the place to look.

Every fee change from here on gets its own short Fee Watch story, so you won't have to wait for a roundup. Earlier from the desk: this year's holiday shipping dates, and how to work out your own last order day.

What we checked: Etsy's fee, photo, Purchase Protection and Share & Save pages, USPS's own price announcements, Mercari's label page, the EU and Irish customs pages, eBay's new balance terms and the IRS 1099-K page. Most were read on October 27, 2026, and each one is listed below with its date.

item.title: Etsy's holiday shipping page still shows last year's dates. Here are this year's
item.description: Planning your Christmas cut-off from Etsy's help page? Its dates and surcharges still matched last December's when we checked, and two of them will cost you this year. Here's the real 2026 calendar, and how to find your own last order day.
item.content:encoded:
The short version: Etsy's help page for holiday shipping cut-offs still showed last December's dates when we checked it on October 22. For Priority Mail Express, that puts you a day late: Etsy says December 20, USPS says December 19. The page also understates the holiday postage rise. Below are this year's dates from the carriers themselves, and how to work out the last day a buyer can order from you.

It's the time of year when Etsy sellers start counting backwards from Christmas. Plenty of them will start where Etsy points them: a help page called "Understanding Shipping Carrier Surcharges & Cutoff Dates for the Holidays".

We read it on October 22 and compared it with a copy the Internet Archive saved on December 14, 2025. Every US date and surcharge note was the same, word for word. Christmas is still on the 25th. Several of the other numbers have moved.

Who can ignore this: shops that only sell digital downloads, and anyone who's already set their holiday cut-off from the carriers' own pages.

Two of last year's numbers will cost you

The Express date. Etsy's page says Priority Mail Express can go as late as December 20. This year USPS says December 19. If your buyer paid for Express so a gift arrives in time, the 20th is one day beyond USPS's recommended send-by date.

The postage rise. Etsy's page says Ground Advantage goes up "$.30-$.35" for the holidays. The real rise is bigger, and it has already started: USPS's holiday prices began on October 4 and run until January 17.

At USPS's commercial rates (its business prices for postage), a small parcel up to 3 lb now costs 40 cents more to nearby zones and 55 cents more to distant ones. Check what your own label service quotes.

That gap sounds small until you multiply it by a December's orders. And Etsy takes its 6.5% transaction fee on what buyers pay for shipping too (Etsy fees), so postage you don't pass on comes straight out of your margin.

The other differences mostly run the safe way. For UPS 3 Day Select and FedEx Express Saver, Etsy's page says December 19. Both carriers now say December 21, so Etsy's dates just cost you two selling days. Etsy's page says it will keep updating the list, so it may well change. Until it does, use the carriers' own dates.

This year's dates, from the carriers

USPS aims for delivery before Christmas Day. UPS and FedEx publish dates for delivery by Thursday, December 24. These are the dates to plan around, within the lower 48 states:

ServiceSend by
USPS Ground Advantage, First-Class MailThu, Dec 17
USPS Priority MailFri, Dec 18
USPS Priority Mail ExpressSat, Dec 19
UPS 3 Day Select / FedEx Express SaverMon, Dec 21
UPS 2nd Day Air / FedEx 2DayTue, Dec 22
UPS Next Day Air / FedEx OvernightWed, Dec 23
UPS Ground / FedEx GroundDepends on the route: Dec 17 for a 5-day FedEx route, later for shorter ones

Sources: USPS, UPS and FedEx. All three say their dates can change.

Shipping to Alaska or Hawaii? Priority and Express use the same dates. Ground Advantage has no date at all: USPS says to allow 10 days or more and to look up your exact ZIP codes. You'll see "December 16" quoted in some news reports. We couldn't find it on either USPS page.

Your real deadline is earlier than any of these

Here's the part most holiday guides skip. The carrier's date is when the parcel has to leave. The date that matters to your shop is the last day a buyer can order.

Etsy works out a buyer's delivery estimate as your processing time plus the carrier's transit time (Etsy Help). So count back from the carrier's date by your processing time. If your listings say 3 to 5 working days, count back 5. The table assumes you process orders Monday to Friday; if your shop also works weekends, your dates come a little later.

Your processing timeLast order day, Ground AdvantageLast order day, Priority Mail
1 working dayWed, Dec 16Thu, Dec 17
2 working daysTue, Dec 15Wed, Dec 16
3 working daysMon, Dec 14Tue, Dec 15
4 working daysFri, Dec 11Mon, Dec 14
5 working daysThu, Dec 10Fri, Dec 11

So a shop promising 5 working days by Ground Advantage should stop promising Christmas on December 10, a full week before the date on everyone's lips. These are planning dates, not a guarantee: parcels do run late in December, so leave a day spare.

Getting this right matters beyond Christmas. Etsy expects at least 80% of your orders to ship within the processing time you set, and shops that fall short can lose search visibility (Etsy Help). Choosing a processing time you can hit in your busiest week, as well as the quiet ones, is one of the first set-up decisions Etsy Basics walks you through.

What to do this week

  1. Write down your last order day from the table, using your longest processing time.
  2. Tell buyers. Put it in your shop announcement and an order-by line in your listings.
  3. Check your shipping price still covers the label. Pull one holiday postage quote for a typical order, then put it, and what you charge for shipping, into our free fee calculator for Etsy sellers. It shows what's left after postage and every Etsy fee.
  4. Shipping to Alaska or Hawaii by Ground Advantage? Look up the ZIP codes on USPS's delivery-time tool now.

We'll check Etsy's page again before December and update this story if it changes. Earlier from the desk: Etsy is quietly paying part of some buyers' shipping, and what it means for your fees.

What we checked: the USPS, UPS and FedEx holiday pages and price lists, Etsy's help pages, and the Internet Archive's copy of Etsy's page, all read on October 22, 2026. Every source is listed below.

item.title: Etsy is paying part of some US buyers' shipping. Your earnings and fees stay the same
item.description: Etsy is testing a cap on what some US buyers pay for calculated shipping, and covering the gap itself. Etsy has now confirmed your fees are still worked out on the full shipping amount, so nothing changes for you.
item.content:encoded:
Updated October 23, 2026: Etsy has answered the open question in our first version of this story. Fees are still charged on the full shipping amount, so there's no saving, and no loss, for you. We've rewritten the story around that answer.

The short version: Etsy is testing a cap on what some US buyers pay for calculated shipping, and Etsy pays the difference. Your item and shipping earnings stay the same, and so do your fees. You don't need to change anything.

Who can ignore this: shops that charge a fixed shipping price or offer free shipping. The test only touches orders that use calculated shipping.

What Etsy is doing

Etsy has emailed US sellers about a "limited, temporary, randomized" test. On some eligible orders that use calculated shipping, the buyer is charged a lower, capped shipping price, and Etsy covers the gap. The test is expected to run for a few weeks.

Etsy's own example, from the email as reproduced by Value Added Resource: your calculated shipping rate is $10, and the buyer is charged a capped $7.99.

You still receive the full $10. Etsy pays the other $2.01. Caps vary by order; $7.99 is the highest one Etsy is testing.

Your fees don't change either

When the test was first reported, nobody knew whether Etsy's fees would be charged on your full $10 or on the $7.99 the buyer paid. Etsy has now told Value Added Resource that transaction and payment-processing fees are still calculated on the full shipping amount, Etsy's share included.

So an order in the test looks exactly like a normal one from your side: same earnings, same fees. The only difference is that your buyer paid a little less for shipping, and Etsy made up the gap.

How you'll know an order was in the test

The difference shows as "Etsy-funded shipping" in that order's Order Details. Your Payment Account still shows your normal shipping revenue. Etsy says no listing or shipping-setting changes are needed. The reports don't say whether a shop can opt out.

Why Etsy is doing this

Etsy has said before that high shipping prices put buyers off. Since 2024 it has favored eligible US listings with shipping under $6 in search, but listings on calculated shipping were left out of that change, as Value Added Resource reported at the time.

This test looks like Etsy checking whether a cheaper shipping price brings more sales to calculated-shipping shops, with Etsy paying for it rather than you. Etsy says the results may inform future improvements to shipping. It hasn't said what those might be, and that's the part worth watching.

What to do

  1. Nothing to change. Keep your calculated shipping as it is.
  2. Watch your Order Details for "Etsy-funded shipping", so you know if your shop is in the test.
  3. Know your real take-home on a normal order. If shipping is a big part of your price, put one order into the free fee calculator for Etsy sellers. It shows what Etsy leaves you after every fee, shipping included.

We'll update this story if Etsy changes the test or says what comes next. Next from the desk: Etsy's holiday shipping page still shows last year's dates, with this year's from the carriers.
